clue.text: Diversions for rubber producers

blocks.note: first meaning: pastimes, amusements
second meaning: in bridge or tennis a rubber is a series decided by winning a set number of these

explanation.surface: Plantations of rubber trees are offered some light entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber producers' points to trees or plantations, but a rubber here is the best-of-three contest in bridge or whist.
explanation.definitionFit: Sports and pastimes are diversions, and a rubber at cards is made up of them.

clue.text: Sponsor film

blocks.note: first meaning: a man who stands sponsor at a christening
second meaning: Coppola's 1972 Mafia picture

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sponsor' suggests backing a film financially, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A male baptismal sponsor carries this title, and it is also the name of the famous gangster movie.

clue.text: Result of end of cooling in mother earth's under-crust

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: an informal word for mother
the last letter of cooling
the second half of the doubled form, as in mama

explanation.surface: A geology lesson on what happens beneath Mother Earth's crust as things cool.
explanation.walkthrough: Mother is taken as MAMA, and the G goes into its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Molten rock lying beneath the solid crust of the planet is called this; cooled, it forms igneous rock.

clue.text: In point-to-point, a new horse seen alongside bay

definitions.note: describes where the answer lies rather than naming it

indicators.note: a new version of a word has its letters made over in a fresh order

blocks.note: two compass points, south and east
taken as written
the five letters of horse rearranged

explanation.surface: At a point-to-point steeplechase, a fresh bay horse is spotted among the runners.
explanation.walkthrough: A point-to-point is a British amateur horse race over fences, and bay is a horse colour, so the surface is all racing; here the points are compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: The strip of land by the sea is what runs beside any bay or cove.

clue.text: Joined in mass, sort of solace church's given to hundreds

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant, so the letters are formed into another arrangement

blocks.note: the six letters of solace rearranged
CE is the Church of England
D is the Roman numeral 500, five hundreds

explanation.surface: Someone describes comfort being handed out by the church to the hundreds who need it.
explanation.definitionFit: To coalesce is to fuse or merge into one body, so things that have done it have united into a mass.

clue.text: One imprisoned as murderer

blocks.note: surface reading: any convicted killer serving a sentence
setter's reading: the first murderer of all, from Genesis; and the numeral for one sits locked inside a can, slang for prison

explanation.walkthrough: The I for 'one' sits inside CAN, slang for jail, which supports the Biblical killer of Abel.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis names Adam's elder son as the first person ever to kill, slaying his brother Abel.

clue.text: Strike, say, bringing countries together

definitions.note: a phrase describing the answer's effect

blocks.note: first meaning: a stoppage is one example of something a trade union does
second meaning: the legislation of 1707 or 1800 joining Britain's nations

explanation.walkthrough: The 1707 statute merged England and Scotland, and that of 1800 added Ireland; read literally, the phrase is any deed by a trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament's statutes uniting Scotland and later Ireland with England bear this name, and a walkout is literally a deed done by organised labour.

clue.text: The sprite's last to start showing wit

indicators.note: the final letter is moved round to the front of the word

blocks.note: a sprite is a fairy or elf; that the answer also runs across these words is a coincidence, since 'last to start' is the instruction

explanation.surface: A mischievous fairy starts to display a sense of humour.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'The' and the possessive are surface dressing; only the word sprite is worked on.
explanation.definitionFit: French borrowing meaning liveliness of mind and sparkling cleverness, a close synonym of quickness in humour.

clue.text: Cats' concert as London alternative to 22 dn

blocks.note: first meaning: a din of banging pans and jeering, like caterwauling
second meaning: the subtitle of the humorous magazine, 'or the London ...'

explanation.walkthrough: Cats' concert might suggest the musical Cats, but it means a discordant racket. Punch magazine's full title was 'Punch, or the London Charivari'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a noisy mock serenade of pots and pans was borrowed into the masthead of the satirical weekly.

clue.text: Live comfortably after 14

indicators.note: what comes after the cross-referenced title is its closing letter, which is the one kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the novel's title at 14 across
living comfortably means living well

explanation.surface: A note that life became comfortable once some event had passed.
explanation.walkthrough: The 14 across title itself ends with END, so 'after 14' takes its end letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside or inhabit a place is to make one's home there, a verb used just as 'live' is.

clue.text: The law he lays down to-follow is in short book

definitions.note: the clue's inversion of 'he lays down the law'

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits within it

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them
an abbreviation for the Gospel of Matthew
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone insists the rule he lays down must be followed, as written in a little book.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is inverted from 'he lays down the law'; 'short book' uses the standard abbreviation for the Gospel of Matthew.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who asserts opinions as undeniable truth is said to lay down the law, the hallmark of this person.

clue.text: Has put in training for a certain period

indicators.note: something put in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: PE is physical education, school training
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone has spent a fixed stretch of time in training.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage or distinct stretch of time in a process, as with the moon's monthly cycle.

clue.text: Passivity shown in a way unknown to mathematicians

blocks.note: taken as written
a way or track
algebra uses x, y and z for unknown quantities

explanation.surface: Mathematicians are mocked for an unfamiliar, inactive approach.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of interest or enthusiasm leaves a person inert and unmoved, which is a passive state.

clue.text: Rupert's English rose wasn't so formal

blocks.note: surface reading: a flower in a poem was rather casual
setter's reading: in Rupert Brooke's Grantchester poem the rose is described with the negative of the answer, so it lacked that quality

explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Brooke's 1912 poem 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester' has the line 'Unkempt about those hedges blows / An English unofficial rose'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done with proper authority or in a prescribed, ceremonial way is both authorised and formal.

clue.text: Possibly take rap, it's said, for bloomer

indicators.note: possibly signals one of several arrangements the letters might take

blocks.note: all the letters of these words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is perhaps blamed, as rumour has it, for a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is British slang for a blunder, which fits taking the rap, but here it is literally something that blooms. The aspidistra was the classic Victorian parlour pot plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer read literally is anything that flowers, and this leafy houseplant does produce blooms.

clue.text: Novel as Catherine losing her head

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman named Catherine panicking
setter's reading: Catherine Howard, fifth wife of Henry VIII, was beheaded in 1542, so this describes her demise

explanation.walkthrough: E. M. Forster's 1910 novel shares its title with a description of what happened to Henry VIII's fifth queen.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a fictional house in Forster's well-known book about the Schlegel and Wilcox families.

clue.text: Naturalist has flower put out to stop shooting

blocks.note: Gilbert White, eighteenth-century English naturalist of Selborne
the flag is a kind of iris

explanation.surface: A nature-lover has a bloom set out in a garden, perhaps to keep pests from new shoots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shooting' looks botanical beside 'flower', but it is gunfire.
explanation.definitionFit: Waving a pale banner signals surrender or truce, so it is displayed to ask for an end to firing.

clue.text: Prince's portrait painter

blocks.note: Prince Hal, Shakespeare's young Henry V
the possessive ending

explanation.surface: An artist who painted a picture of a prince.
explanation.definitionFit: Frans Hals was the Dutch Golden Age master famed for lively portraits like The Laughing Cavalier.

clue.text: This writer given another spell as railwayman

indicators.note: spelling a name another way keeps how it is said while changing how it looks

blocks.note: George Stephenson, pioneer of steam railways and the Rocket

explanation.surface: An author gets a second turn, this time working on the railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell' suggests a period of time, but here it is spelling: change PH to V.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis, author of Treasure Island and Kidnapped, is the novelist bearing this surname.

clue.text: It's hard to fire, for instance, first rounds

blocks.note: as in 'such as'
first place is the best
the letter O is round, so rounds are Os

explanation.surface: A gunnery note that the opening rounds are difficult to shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' and 'rounds' suggest guns, but the fire means burning.
explanation.definitionFit: This mineral fibre resists heat and flame, so it is difficult to set alight.

clue.text: Rule pronounced right in comparison

indicators.note: pronounced means we go by what is said aloud, not by spelling

blocks.note: the comparison 'as right as rain'

explanation.surface: A remark that a rule, when spoken, sounds correct by comparison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule' tempts one to try reign, but the sound-alike comes from 'right as rain', the stock comparison for being well.
explanation.definitionFit: To rein something in is to curb or control it, so the verb can mean govern or keep in check.

clue.text: Small but generous contribution for orphan

definitions.note: a child who has lost its father

blocks.note: first meaning: from Mark's Gospel, the poor woman's two small coins, which were all she had
second meaning: a mite is a small child, and one whose mother is bereaved has lost a father

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a charity gift for an orphan, but 'orphan' is a second definition: a mite is a little child.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gospel phrase means a modest gift that is large relative to the giver's means; read literally it is a bereaved mother's little one.

clue.text: Brand X's natural successor in this French town?

definitions.text: Brand X's natural successor in this French town?

blocks.note: surface reading: the product that follows an unnamed advertised brand
setter's reading: Y naturally follows X, so brand followed by Y is the spirit distilled in this Charente town

explanation.walkthrough: In adverts Brand X is the anonymous rival product; change X to the next letter and it becomes brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in western France gives its name to the region's famous grape brandy.

clue.text: A pierrot doing a turn? Capital

indicators.note: doing a turn suggests tumbling about, so the letters are rolled into a new order

blocks.note: all the letters of these words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A clown performing his act on stage: is it first-rate?
explanation.walkthrough: A pierrot is a sad-faced clown, and a turn is a stage act; 'Capital!' as an exclamation means excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: The South African city is the country's administrative seat of government.

clue.text: Magazine on hand to entertain the children

definitions.text: on hand to entertain the children

blocks.note: first meaning: the British satirical weekly

blocks.clueFragment: on hand to entertain the children
blocks.note: second meaning: the glove puppet of the seaside show with Judy

explanation.walkthrough: Punch and Judy is a traditional British seaside puppet show; the puppeteer wears the puppet literally on his hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The humorous weekly took its name from the hook-nosed puppet hero of the children's booth show.

clue.text: Animal responsible for Darwin's main progress

blocks.note: first meaning: a small hunting hound
second meaning: the naval ship that carried the naturalist around the world

explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the sea, as in the Spanish Main, so Darwin's progress over it was aboard HMS Beagle; the surface suggests his chief advance in theory.
explanation.definitionFit: The scent hound is an animal, and HMS of that name carried the naturalist on his voyage.

clue.text: Whence the good news, initially perhaps

definitions.text: Whence the good news, initially perhaps

blocks.clueFragment: Whence the good news, initially perhaps
blocks.note: surface reading: the source of the gospel or of some happy tidings

blocks.clueFragment: Whence the good news, initially perhaps
blocks.note: setter's reading: Browning's poem 'How They Brought the Good News from ... to Aix' names the Flemish city where the ride began

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Browning's galloping poem starts in a Belgian city and ends at Aix; 'perhaps' admits the news is never specified.
explanation.definitionFit: This Flemish city is the starting point in Browning's ride, so the tidings came from there at first.

clue.text: A prophet 'e's abandoned for another

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for a second prophet, fair because the wordplay has just named one

indicators.note: letters that are abandoned are left out of the word

blocks.note: taken as written
the lawgiver of Exodus
the letters e and s, written as a dropped-aitch 'he's'

explanation.surface: A prophet, in Cockney, has gone off and left one behind for a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: ''e's' looks like Cockney for 'he's', but it is simply the letters E and S, removed from the end of MOSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Another Old Testament seer, a shepherd from Tekoa with a short book of the minor prophets named after him.

clue.text: Tony longs to use this material in clothes

indicators.note: the words before are put to use as a source, with the letters taken from inside them

blocks.note: running across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A man called Tony yearns to wear a certain synthetic fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Longs' looks like the verb of desire; it also hints at stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: The synthetic polymer fibre was used for stockings and much other clothing from the 1940s on.

clue.text: She-devil?

blocks.note: surface reading: a female fiend or a vicious woman
setter's reading: the devil is the tempter, so his female counterpart is a woman who lures

explanation.walkthrough: The Devil is traditionally called the Tempter; the question mark admits the female form is a playful stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A seductive woman who entices others is the feminine counterpart of the tempter, a name for Satan.

clue.text: Superior Oxford Street set

blocks.note: the High is the main street of Oxford
a set or group

explanation.surface: Smart people from London's Oxford Street are considered a cut above.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford Street suggests London's shopping street, but here it is a street in Oxford: the High.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of top quality or social standing is described as superior in rank or grade.

clue.text: Fabric demonstrated, by way of occupation

definitions.note: read as two words, a verb phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: a smooth, glossy cloth
second meaning: protested by occupying a building, staging a sit-in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Occupation' looks like a job, but it is occupying premises as a protest.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossy woven silk cloth is a fabric; split in two, it gives the past tense of staging a sit-in protest.
